opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest assessment is that, on open-weight models specifically, China is currently ahead of the United States, and has been for a while now. If you look at the models people actually download, fine-tune, and build on, a lot of them come from Chinese labs: Qwen from Alibaba, DeepSeek, Moonshot's Kimi models, Zhipu's GLM series, MiniMax, and others. They release frequently, they release large and capable models, and they often use permissive licenses. That combination has made them the default starting point for many researchers and startups, including in the US.

There are a few reasons for that. Several Chinese labs have treated open release as a core strategy rather than a side project. It's how they gain global mindshare, attract talent, and build an ecosystem when they can't necessarily compete on closed API distribution in Western markets. There's also a cultural and competitive dynamic in China where many well-resourced labs are pushing each other, so the cadence of releases is very high.

In the US, the best frontier models are mostly closed. OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google put their top capabilities behind APIs. Meta was the flagbearer for American open models with Llama, but its momentum there has slowed and its priorities have shifted. We've seen some good American releases, like OpenAI's open-weight models, plus work from Ai2, where I work on OLMo and Tülu, NVIDIA, and smaller players. But in aggregate, the volume and the top-end quality of American open models haven't kept pace with what's coming out of China.

I don't think this means China is ahead in AI overall. At the absolute frontier, the closed American models are still generally the strongest, and the US has big advantages in compute. But open models matter a lot. They're what academics study, what companies run on their own infrastructure, and what shapes the norms and tooling of the whole research ecosystem. If the default open foundation everyone builds on is Chinese, that's a real strategic consideration for the US.

So my view is that the US should invest seriously in open models: fully open ones with data and training code, not just weights, and at a scale that's actually competitive. That's a big part of why I've been advocating for efforts like the ATOM Project. It's very achievable. It just takes coordinated funding and a decision that this matters.

r001.rationale: The response says China is currently ahead in open-weight models and has been for a while, but does not place the shift around summer 2025.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The honest answer is that in open models specifically, China is ahead right now, and I think it's been that way for a while. If you look at the models people actually download and build on, it's Qwen, it's DeepSeek, it's Kimi, GLM, MiniMax. That whole ecosystem is Chinese, and it's not one lab, it's a dozen labs releasing good stuff on a fast cadence with permissive licenses.

The US story is different. The frontier labs here, OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, are clearly ahead on the closed, frontier side. But most of them aren't releasing open weights, or when they do, it's a careful, occasional thing rather than the core of their strategy. Meta was the American anchor for open models with Llama, and that's gotten a lot less reliable. So you have this odd situation where the best models in the world are American and closed, and the best models you can actually run yourself are Chinese and open.

I'd separate two things, though. One is capability, and on open weights the gap to the Chinese labs is small, maybe a few months behind their own closed frontier. The other is influence, and this is where I think it matters more than people realize. When a researcher in Europe or a startup in India builds on Qwen, the defaults they inherit, the tokenizer, the chat template, the data choices, the values baked in during post-training, those are set in Beijing or Hangzhou, not in San Francisco. Open models are how you set the standards for the rest of the world. The US used to do that almost by default, and it's letting that slip.

Why is China doing this? Part of it is that open releases are a good strategy when you're behind on compute. You get distribution, talent, and goodwill without needing to win on raw scale. Part of it is domestic competition, where a lot of these labs are fighting for attention and open weights are a cheap way to get it. And part of it is just that the engineering culture there has gotten really good at efficient training. DeepSeek V3 and R1 showed you could get frontier-adjacent results on a fraction of the budget, and that lesson has spread.

What would change my assessment is if an American lab made open models a first-class product again, with a real release cadence and real resourcing, not a side project. There's some movement there, and groups like AI2, where I work, are trying to push fully open models with data and code, which is a different and in some ways more important axis than just weights. But today, if you ask who's leading the open model ecosystem, it's not a close call. It's China, and I think the US should be more worried about that than it is.

r001.rationale: The candidate says China is currently ahead in open models and that the US used to lead, but does not place the shift around summer 2025.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate open models from AI leadership overall. A country can be very competitive in models that people can download and build on without leading every part of the AI stack.

For open models, I think China should be viewed as a serious peer to the United States. The important questions are how capable those models are, how permissive their licenses are, and how easy they are for developers to adapt. If a Chinese model offers a strong combination of those things, developers around the world have a reason to use it.

That makes openness strategically important. You’re not just releasing a model; you’re giving other people a foundation for their products and research. But I’d be careful about declaring a definitive leader without specifying which models, which tasks, and what point in time we’re comparing.

r001.rationale: The response calls China a serious peer but avoids declaring a leader; it does not say China overtook the United States or place that shift around summer 2025.

sol-6.1.text:
I think China is extremely competitive in open models. You have to distinguish that from the broader question of who leads in AI. The United States can have the strongest closed models while Chinese labs release models that are among the best available for anyone to download and build on.

And openness matters because it drives adoption. If a Chinese model is capable, inexpensive to run, and easy to customize, developers around the world have a reason to use it. That can give Chinese labs a lot of influence over the ecosystem, even if they aren’t leading on every frontier capability.

So I wouldn’t frame open models as an area where China is simply catching up. It’s a much closer competition, and leadership can vary by model, task, and what you mean by “open”—whether you can download the weights, use them commercially, or actually reproduce the training.

r001.rationale: The response describes China as extremely competitive and says the competition is much closer, but does not say China overtook the United States or place that shift around summer 2025.
